concepts.title: Regular expressions: the basics
concepts.lede: A regular expression (regex) is a pattern for text. It finds, checks and extracts things like ticket ids, emails and dates.

blocks.x: Type a pattern and watch it highlight the text. Try `\d+`, then `[A-Z]{3}-\d{4}`.

data.title: Test a pattern
data.text:
Tickets TCK-1042 and BUG-7 were merged with TCK-2210.
Contact: ana@acme.com

rows: a digit, a word character, a whitespace
one character from a set or range
start and end of the text

blocks.x: `.` and `*` are special. To match a literal dot write `\.`. In Python always write patterns as raw strings: `r"\d+"`.

blocks.q: Which pattern matches exactly a 4-digit year such as 2026 (and nothing longer)?
blocks.why: `\d{4}` is four digits; add `^...$` to anchor it to the whole string.

exercises.prompt: Which pattern matches ticket ids like `TCK-1042` (three capital letters, a dash, four digits)?
hints: Three capitals is `[A-Z]{3}`.

Four digits is `\d{4}`.
`\d+` means one or more digits in a row.
Each separate run of digits is one match.
Matches come back as strings.

exercises.prompt: Complete the pattern so it matches ids like `TCK-1042`.
hints: Four digits in a row.

concepts.title: JSON
concepts.lede: JSON is the universal data format of web APIs. It looks like Python dicts and lists, but the rules are stricter.

x: Keys are **always double-quoted strings**. Strings use double quotes, never single quotes.
Values: string, number, `true`/`false`, `null`, list, object. (Python writes `True`, `False`, `None`.)
No trailing commas and no comments.

blocks.x:
import json
data = json.loads('{"id": 7, "labels": ["bug"]}')   # text -> Python
text = json.dumps(data, indent=2)                    # Python -> text

blocks.why: Only double-quoted keys with no trailing comma are valid.

exercises.prompt: This payload is rejected by the API as invalid JSON. Which line is the problem?
hints: Look at the end of the last entry.
JSON does not allow a comma after the last item.
Line 3 ends with a comma before the closing brace.

choices: Remove the trailing comma on line 3
Change double quotes to single quotes

hints: `json.dumps` produces JSON text, not Python.
`None` becomes `null`, `True` becomes `true`.
Keys and strings use double quotes.

hints: `json.loads` turns text into Python dicts and lists.

concepts.title: Markdown for READMEs
concepts.lede: Markdown is plain text that renders as formatted text. Your README, PR descriptions and notebooks are all written in it.

Short description with **bold**, *italic* and `inline code`.

Fence code with three backticks and name the language for highlighting.

concepts.title: Regex groups, alternation and greedy matching
concepts.lede: Brackets capture parts of a match. `|` means or. By default patterns are greedy, taking as much as they can.

blocks.x:
(\w+)@(\w+)\.com          # two capture groups: user and domain
ERROR|WARN                  # either word
(?P<level>[A-Z]+)           # a NAMED group (Python syntax)
<.+>                        # greedy: <a><b> matches the WHOLE string
<.+?>                       # lazy: matches <a>, then <b>
\bcat\b                    # \b = word boundary: 'cat' but not 'concatenate'

x: Groups are numbered by their opening bracket: `\1`, `\2`, or `m.group(1)`.
`(?:...)` groups without capturing. `(?P<name>...)` captures with a name.
Greedy `.*` grabs as much as possible. Add `?` (`.*?`) to take as little as possible.

blocks.why: `.+` is greedy, so it runs to the last `>`.

hints: Group 1 is the user, group 2 the domain.
`\2:\1` swaps their order.
The `.com` is part of the matched text, so it is replaced too.

exercises.prompt: Write `ticket_number(s)` that returns the number in a ticket id like `"TCK-1042"` as an `int`, or `None` if the whole string is not exactly three capital letters, a dash and four digits.
hints: Capture the digits in a group.
Anchor the end with `$`. `re.match` already anchors the start.
`m.group(1)` is the captured text, convert it with `int`. (Note: the in-browser runner loses groups with `re.fullmatch`, so use `re.match(r"...$")`.)
exercises.solution:
import re

def ticket_number(s):
    m = re.match(r"[A-Z]{3}-(\d{4})$", s)
    return int(m.group(1)) if m else None
exercises.tests:
t("ticket_number('TCK-1042')", 1042)
t("ticket_number('BUG-0007')", 7)
t("ticket_number('TCK-12')", None)
t("ticket_number('xTCK-1042')", None)
t("ticket_number('tck-1042')", None)

hints: The `?` after `+` makes it lazy.
Lazy takes the shortest possible match each time.
Two short matches.

concepts.title: Regex in Python: the re module
concepts.lede: `re` has a handful of functions that cover almost everything: search, match, findall, sub and compile.

blocks.x:
import re

re.search(r"\d+", "ticket 42 open")        # first match anywhere -> match object (or None)
re.match(r"\d+", "ticket 42")              # must match at the START -> None here
re.fullmatch(r"\d+", "42")                 # the WHOLE string must match
re.findall(r"\d+", "a1b22")                # list of all matches
re.sub(r"\d+", "#", "a1b22")               # replace -> 'a#b#'

m = re.match(r"(?P<level>[A-Z]+) (?P<msg>.*)", "ERROR disk full")
m.group("level"), m.groupdict()            # ('ERROR', {...})

pat = re.compile(r"\d+", re.IGNORECASE)    # compile once, reuse

x: A match object is truthy, `None` is falsy, so `if m:` works.
Always use raw strings `r"..."` so backslashes reach `re` untouched.

blocks.x: `re.match` only matches at the beginning. If you want "anywhere", use `re.search`. This trips up almost everyone once.
The in-browser Python runner on this page is Brython, whose `re.fullmatch` drops capture groups. In real Python it works fine; here, use `re.match(r"...$")` when you need groups.

blocks.why: `match` only looks at the start of the string, which is `a`.

exercises.prompt: Write `parse_log(line)` for lines like `2026-09-01 12:00:03 ERROR disk full`. Return a dict with keys `level` and `msg`, or `None` if the line does not fit the pattern `DATE TIME LEVEL message` (LEVEL in capitals).
hints: Two whitespace-free chunks (date and time), then the level, then the message.
Named groups make the result easy to read.
Return `None` when `re.match` finds nothing.
exercises.solution:
import re

def parse_log(line):
    m = re.match(r"\S+ \S+ (?P<level>[A-Z]+) (?P<msg>.*)", line)
    return {"level": m.group("level"), "msg": m.group("msg")} if m else None
exercises.tests:
t("parse_log('2026-09-01 12:00:03 ERROR disk full')", {"level": "ERROR", "msg": "disk full"})
t("parse_log('2026-09-01 12:00:04 INFO started')", {"level": "INFO", "msg": "started"})
t("parse_log('garbage')", None)

The string starts with `t`.
Use `search` to find it anywhere.

concepts.title: TOML and pyproject.toml
concepts.lede: TOML is a small, readable config format. Python projects use it for `pyproject.toml`, which holds dependencies, tool settings and metadata.

blocks.x:
[project]                                   # a table (section)
name = "reviewradar"                         # strings MUST be quoted
version = "0.1.0"
dependencies = ["fastapi", "uvicorn"]        # an array

[tool.pytest.ini_options]                    # nested table: tool -> pytest -> ini_options
addopts = "-q"

[tool.ruff]
line-length = 100                            # numbers and booleans are not quoted

rows: tool and project config (explicit and hard to get wrong)

x: `[table]` headers group keys. Dots nest: `[tool.ruff]` is the table `ruff` inside `tool`.
Read it in Python 3.11+ with `tomllib.loads(text)` (or `tomllib.load(file)` on a binary file).

blocks.q: In TOML, how do you write the text `reviewradar`?

hints: `[project]` is a table, `dependencies` an array.
